missions/pauline-mission/statusNote: Paul's churches outlived him and his letters became Scripture; his mission ended with his death in Rome (c. 64–67 by tradition), but its theology and methods were absorbed into, and endlessly reinterpreted by, the wider church.
missions/pauline-mission/summary: The mission of Paul of Tarsus, a Pharisee turned apostle, and his team of co-workers, who between the late 40s and c. 60 founded house churches in the cities of Cyprus, Galatia, Macedonia, Achaia and Asia, arguing that Gentiles were justified by faith in Christ without circumcision. His letters — the earliest surviving Christian documents — and Luke's Acts make it the best-documented mission of antiquity.
missions/pauline-mission/story:
Saul, a Greek-speaking Jew from Tarsus trained as a Pharisee, persecuted the followers of Jesus until a vision of the risen Christ near Damascus (c. 33–34) convinced him that he had been called as an apostle to the Gentiles. He spent some time in ‘Arabia’ (the Nabataean kingdom), returned to Damascus, escaped the ethnarch of King Aretas, visited Peter in Jerusalem, and then worked for roughly a decade in Syria and his native Cilicia — a period about which almost nothing is known. Around 44 Barnabas brought him to Antioch, the first city where Jews and Gentiles worshipped together in large numbers.

The Antioch church sent Barnabas and Saul, with Barnabas's cousin John Mark, on what is conventionally called the first missionary journey (c. 46–48). They crossed Cyprus, where Acts claims the conversion of the proconsul Sergius Paulus, and then struck inland to the Roman colonies of southern Galatia — Pisidian Antioch, Iconium, Lystra and Derbe. The pattern set here recurred: preaching first in the synagogue, gaining a following among Jews and especially God-fearing Gentiles, expulsion or violence (Paul was stoned and left for dead at Lystra), and the appointment of elders before moving on. The success among Gentiles provoked the controversy over circumcision that the Jerusalem meeting (c. 48/49) resolved in Paul's favour, though the subsequent quarrel at Antioch broke his partnership with Barnabas.

On the second journey (c. 49–52) Paul, now with Silas and Timothy, revisited Galatia and then, blocked from Asia and Bithynia, crossed from Troas to Macedonia — the first recorded Christian mission in Europe. Churches were founded in Philippi (with the merchant Lydia), Thessalonica and Beroea; Paul was mocked at Athens but stayed eighteen months in Corinth, working as a tentmaker with the refugee couple Priscilla and Aquila. The proconsul Gallio's refusal to hear charges against him (inscription dated 51–52) provides the key fixed point of Pauline chronology. From Corinth he wrote 1 Thessalonians, probably the oldest Christian text.

The third journey (c. 53–57) centred on Ephesus, where Paul taught daily for two years in the lecture hall of Tyrannus and from which co-workers planted churches in the Lycus valley (Colossae, Laodicea, Hierapolis). These were years of crisis: rival missionaries in Galatia demanding circumcision, factions and moral disputes at Corinth, imprisonment (probably in Ephesus) and the riot of the silversmiths. The great letters — Galatians, 1–2 Corinthians, Philippians, Philemon and finally Romans — date from this period. Paul's last project was a collection from his Gentile churches for the poor of Jerusalem, a symbol of the unity of Jew and Gentile.

Arrested in the Temple on delivering the collection (c. 57), Paul was held for two years at Caesarea before appealing to Caesar. The voyage to Rome (c. 59–60), narrated vividly in Acts 27–28, ended in shipwreck on Malta; he reached Rome and lived two years under house arrest, preaching openly. Acts ends there. 1 Clement (c. 96) says he reached ‘the limits of the West’ — possibly Spain, which he had planned to visit — and was martyred; tradition dates his beheading to Nero's reign (c. 64–67).

Paul's mission was small in numbers — perhaps a few thousand believers in a dozen or more cities by his death — but disproportionate in effect. His letters entered the New Testament; his insistence that Gentiles need not become Jews shaped Christianity's identity; and his methods (urban centres, mobile teams, self-support, quick transfer of leadership to local elders) became a recurring reference point, most explicitly in Roland Allen's Missionary Methods: St Paul's or Ours? (1912). His theology has also been the most contested in Christian history, from Marcion to Augustine, Luther and the ‘New Perspective’.
missions/pauline-mission/beliefs/0: God's righteousness is revealed in the death and resurrection of Jesus, through whom both Jews and Gentiles are put right with God by faith rather than by works of the Law.
missions/pauline-mission/beliefs/1: In Christ ‘there is neither Jew nor Greek, slave nor free, male and female’ (Galatians 3:28) — one body formed by baptism and the Spirit.
missions/pauline-mission/beliefs/2: The risen Jesus is Lord, whose imminent return will raise the dead and complete salvation.
missions/pauline-mission/beliefs/3: Gentile converts should not be circumcised or adopt the Jewish food laws, but must abandon idolatry and sexual immorality.
missions/pauline-mission/beliefs/4: The Holy Spirit gives gifts (prophecy, tongues, teaching, healing) to every member for the building up of the church.
missions/pauline-mission/beliefs/5: God has not abandoned Israel; Paul hoped that ‘all Israel will be saved’ (Romans 11).
missions/pauline-mission/strategies/0: Concentrating on Roman provincial capitals and colonies on main roads and sea routes (Thessalonica, Corinth, Ephesus) from which the message could radiate.
missions/pauline-mission/strategies/1: Beginning in synagogues, where God-fearing Gentiles formed a bridge audience.
missions/pauline-mission/strategies/2: Self-support by manual labour as a tentmaker or leatherworker, to avoid dependence on patrons.
missions/pauline-mission/strategies/3: Working with a mobile team of co-workers — Barnabas, Silas, Timothy, Titus, Priscilla and Aquila, Phoebe, Junia and others — including women leaders.
missions/pauline-mission/strategies/4: Meeting in households, using the patronage networks of hosts such as Lydia, Gaius and Philemon.
missions/pauline-mission/strategies/5: Staying weeks or months, appointing elders, and then supervising by letters, envoys and return visits.
missions/pauline-mission/strategies/6: The collection for Jerusalem as an expression of unity and reciprocity between Gentile and Jewish churches.
missions/pauline-mission/groupsReached/0: Diaspora Jews in the synagogues of Asia Minor and Greece.
missions/pauline-mission/groupsReached/1: God-fearers: Gentiles attached to synagogues who welcomed a Law-free route into God's people.
missions/pauline-mission/groupsReached/2: Urban artisans, traders and freedpeople, with some higher-status householders (Erastus the city treasurer, Gaius, Crispus the synagogue ruler).
missions/pauline-mission/groupsReached/3: Slaves and their owners, sometimes in the same congregation (Onesimus and Philemon).
missions/pauline-mission/groupsReached/4: Women of means who hosted and led churches (Lydia, Chloe, Phoebe, Nympha).
missions/pauline-mission/groupsReached/5: Pagans turned ‘from idols to serve a living and true God’ (1 Thessalonians 1:9), notably in Thessalonica and Corinth.
missions/pauline-mission/challenges/0: Violent opposition from synagogue authorities and city crowds: beatings, stoning at Lystra, imprisonment at Philippi and probably Ephesus (2 Corinthians 11 lists five synagogue floggings).
missions/pauline-mission/challenges/1: Rival missionaries who insisted on circumcision (Galatia) or claimed superior spiritual credentials (Corinth).
missions/pauline-mission/challenges/2: Disorder in new churches: factions, lawsuits, sexual immorality and divisions between rich and poor at the Lord's Supper in Corinth.
missions/pauline-mission/challenges/3: The broken partnership with Barnabas and the unresolved Antioch dispute with Peter.
missions/pauline-mission/challenges/4: Suspicion in Jerusalem that Paul taught Jews to abandon the Law, leading to his arrest in 57.
missions/pauline-mission/challenges/5: Travel hazards: shipwreck (three before the voyage to Rome), bandits, hunger and exposure.
missions/pauline-mission/harms/0: Paul's harsh polemic against opponents (e.g. Galatians 5:12; Philippians 3:2) and 1 Thessalonians 2:14–16 were later used to justify Christian hostility to Jews.
missions/pauline-mission/harms/1: His acceptance of slavery as a social given (returning Onesimus; ‘slaves, obey’ in the household codes of Colossians and Ephesians) was cited for centuries to defend slavery.
missions/pauline-mission/harms/2: Passages restricting women's speech and authority (1 Corinthians 14:34–35; 1 Timothy 2:12, whose Pauline authorship is debated) were used to exclude women from ministry, despite the women co-workers in his own letters.
missions/pauline-mission/harms/3: Disputes about his gospel caused lasting division with Jewish believers and within his own churches.
missions/pauline-mission/harms/4: His theology was quickly appropriated by Marcion (c. 144), who rejected the Jewish Scriptures altogether — an outcome Paul did not intend but which shows how open his letters were to anti-Jewish reading.
missions/pauline-mission/developments/0: Thirteen letters (seven undisputed) that became the core of the New Testament and the earliest Christian writings.
missions/pauline-mission/developments/1: The theological rationale for a universal, culture-crossing faith not bound to one ethnic law.
missions/pauline-mission/developments/2: A durable model of urban church planting with quickly appointed local leadership, revived in modern missiology by Roland Allen and others.
missions/pauline-mission/developments/3: The first churches in Europe (Philippi, Thessalonica, Corinth).
missions/pauline-mission/developments/4: A theology of charismatic gifts and of the church as the body of Christ.
missions/pauline-mission/developments/5: A practice of inter-church solidarity through the Jerusalem collection.
missions/pauline-mission/outcome: Paul died a prisoner, his churches small and often troubled, yet his letters became authoritative Scripture and his mission defined Christianity as a faith for all nations. Every later cross-cultural mission has, consciously or not, argued with his precedent.
missions/pauline-mission/keyPeople/0/ori: Tarsus in Cilicia; Pharisee and Roman citizen
missions/pauline-mission/keyPeople/0/foc: Founding Gentile churches in Galatia, Macedonia, Achaia and Asia; letters
missions/pauline-mission/keyPeople/0/out: Executed in Rome by early tradition, probably under Nero
missions/pauline-mission/keyPeople/1/rol: Paul's sponsor and partner on the first journey
missions/pauline-mission/keyPeople/1/out: Separated from Paul c. 49 over John Mark; worked in Cyprus
missions/pauline-mission/keyPeople/3/ori: Lystra; son of a Jewish mother and Greek father
missions/pauline-mission/keyPeople/3/out: Remembered by tradition as first bishop of Ephesus
missions/pauline-mission/keyPeople/4/ori: Jewish tentmakers expelled from Rome under Claudius
missions/pauline-mission/keyPeople/4/out: Hosted house churches in Ephesus and Rome
missions/pauline-mission/keyPeople/5/foc: Carried the Letter to the Romans
missions/pauline-mission/keyPeople/6/foc: Corinth, the collection; by tradition Crete
missions/pauline-mission/keyPeople/6/out: Uncircumcised test case at the Jerusalem meeting
missions/pauline-mission/countries/0/tex: After his conversion Paul worked for about a decade around Tarsus and Antioch; Antioch became his sending church.
missions/pauline-mission/countries/1/tex: Paul spent a period in ‘Arabia’ (Galatians 1:17), probably the Nabataean kingdom; whether he preached there is unknown.
missions/pauline-mission/countries/2/tex: First stage of the first journey: preaching from Salamis to Paphos, where Acts reports the proconsul Sergius Paulus believed.
missions/pauline-mission/countries/3/tex: Churches in Pisidian Antioch, Iconium, Lystra and Derbe; later the target of rival missionaries demanding circumcision, provoking the Letter to the Galatians.
missions/pauline-mission/countries/4/tex: First recorded churches in Europe at Philippi, Thessalonica and Beroea; the Philippians supported Paul financially.
missions/pauline-mission/countries/5/tex: A small response in Athens; an 18-month stay in Corinth produced a large, socially mixed and turbulent church.
missions/pauline-mission/countries/6/tex: Ephesus was Paul's base c. 52–55; co-workers such as Epaphras founded churches at Colossae, Laodicea and Hierapolis.
missions/pauline-mission/countries/7/tex: Shipwrecked on the voyage to Rome, Paul spent three winter months on the island (Acts 28); Maltese Christianity claims him as founder.
missions/pauline-mission/countries/8/tex: Paul wrote to the existing Roman church c. 57 and arrived as a prisoner c. 60, preaching under house arrest; executed there by tradition.
missions/pauline-mission/countries/9/tex: Paul planned a mission to Spain (Romans 15:24). Whether he went, as 1 Clement's ‘limits of the West’ may imply, is debated.
missions/pauline-mission/journeys/0/titl: Conversion and early years: Damascus, Arabia, Jerusalem, Tarsus, Antioch
missions/pauline-mission/journeys/0/text: Converted near Damascus, Paul went to Arabia, returned to Damascus, escaped over the wall in a basket, visited Peter in Jerusalem after three years, and worked in Syria and Cilicia until Barnabas brought him to Antioch (Galatians 1; Acts 9, 11).
missions/pauline-mission/journeys/1/titl: First missionary journey: Cyprus and southern Galatia
missions/pauline-mission/journeys/1/peop: Paul, Barnabas and (as far as Perga) John Mark
missions/pauline-mission/journeys/1/text: Sent out by the Antioch church (Acts 13–14), the team crossed Cyprus, then preached in the synagogues and cities of southern Galatia. Mark turned back at Perga; Paul was stoned at Lystra. Returning by the same route, they appointed elders in each church.
missions/pauline-mission/journeys/2/peop: Paul, Silas, Timothy (and Luke in the ‘we’ passages)
missions/pauline-mission/journeys/2/text: After parting from Barnabas, Paul revisited Galatia, crossed to Macedonia after a vision at Troas, and founded churches at Philippi, Thessalonica and Beroea. He preached at the Areopagus in Athens and spent eighteen months in Corinth (dated by the Gallio inscription, 51–52) before a brief stop in Ephesus (Acts 15:36–18:22).
missions/pauline-mission/journeys/3/titl: Third missionary journey: Ephesus and the collection
missions/pauline-mission/journeys/3/peop: Paul with Timothy, Titus, Erastus and others
missions/pauline-mission/journeys/3/text: Paul spent over two years in Ephesus, then travelled through Macedonia to Corinth, where he wrote Romans. Carrying the collection for Jerusalem, he sailed back by Troas, Miletus and Tyre, and was arrested in the Temple (Acts 18:23–21:36).
missions/pauline-mission/journeys/4/titl: Voyage to Rome as a prisoner
missions/pauline-mission/journeys/4/peop: Paul, Luke and Aristarchus, under the centurion Julius
missions/pauline-mission/journeys/4/text: Having appealed to Caesar, Paul sailed late in the season; a north-easterly gale drove the grain ship fourteen days across the Adriatic to wreck on Malta. After wintering there he continued via Syracuse and Puteoli to Rome, where he lived two years under guard (Acts 27–28).
missions/pauline-mission/relations/0/tex: Paul's churches in Asia, Macedonia, Achaia and Rome became key centres of second- and third-century Christianity; his letters circulated as a collection by c. 100.
missions/pauline-mission/agreements/0/te: The ‘pillars’ James, Peter and John gave Paul and Barnabas ‘the right hand of fellowship’ for the Gentile mission (Galatians 2:9), and Paul honoured Jerusalem through the collection.
missions/pauline-mission/disagreements/0: Paul clashed with Jerusalem-based believers who required circumcision, and publicly opposed Peter at Antioch over withdrawing from table fellowship with Gentiles (Galatians 2:11–14).
missions/pauline-mission/deviations/0: The Pastoral Epistles (1–2 Timothy, Titus), widely regarded as post-Pauline, present a more institutional, hierarchical and socially conservative church than the charismatic communities of the undisputed letters.
missions/pauline-mission/deviations/1: The prominent women co-workers of Romans 16 were progressively written out of leadership in the generations after Paul.
missions/pauline-mission/deviations/2: Paul's hope for the salvation of Israel (Romans 9–11) gave way in later Gentile Christianity to theologies of replacement.
missions/pauline-mission/deviations/3: Marcion's radical Paulinism (c. 144), which rejected the Jewish Scriptures, was condemned by the wider church as a distortion of Paul.
